injury, rape, fear or annoyance is a criminal act, took years; extraordinary courage from one
woman, and an uprising where other women stood in solidarity with her. France has adopted a
law that defines rape as any non-consensual sexual act, a milestone for the women in the
country, but overall, a strike against sexual violence. The law was passed in response to urgent

autonomy, particularly with reference to women. Last year, Gisèle Pelicot fought her toughest
battle when she took the stand in court, in a case accusing her husband of drugging and allowing
her to be raped by several men, some complete strangers. In December last year, the court
granted 51 convictions in the case, but it was more significant for establishing consent as a
pillar of law. It has been well established that survivors of sexual violence have an arduous
journey bringing their case to a court of law, and many women from disadvantaged social and
economic backgrounds, indeed do not have that privilege. There is a great deal of stigma, and

My two-year-old can spot Ambedkar anywhere. On the walls, in the streets, in photographs,
on the television. He’ll also point out if he sees someone wearing “Ambedkar kannadi”. The
same with Gandhi. He’s a Sanjay Subrahmanyan fan, and requests songs any time he meets
Sanjay maama. If only my husband and I could curate who gets to raise our son, we’d fill his
life with people and things that aligned with our beliefs like these. After all, we have curated
our own adult lives this way. Minimising interactions with those we are unable to reconcile
with on the important things. What I have discovered, however, is that it indeed does take a
village to raise a child.


Much as I want to be the primary influencer of his life, he is a being of his own, has always
been. And because he speaks, and he speaks a lot at so young an age, and because he isn’t
anxious about the world, and is looking at it with wonder and love, awe and joy, he has
interactions with several people, many ideas, vastly varied approaches to life every single day.
And it is impossible for me to handpick his world to be only touched by those whose
impeccable taste I approve of. It is his interactions with strangers that bring me the most delight
and, of course, concern.


And so, I’m trying to take the pressure off my son now, and apply it on to my own self — only
this time, to make myself softer. To set the example, by holding myself accountable to others,
I share my space with. By trying to figure out how to not fly into rage, and deal with conflict
with presence and control. To show him how much I love the softer things for him as well.
Embracing the Montessori way has helped somewhat at this stage, for it emphasises

in an act of collective despair has forced a harrowing reckoning with a new, endemic form of
addiction. These children had lived almost entirely within a gaming world for months –
reportedly insulated from reality and withdrawn from school. When their access was abruptly
severed to break the cycle, the resulting “void” proved too much to bear. For them, the scolding
was not merely a lecture; it was a perceived threat to the only domain in which he felt a sense
of achievement and agency. These cases underscore a terrifying reality: when the “digital

What caused this degradation across your favourite platforms and apps? One theory that has

through which internet platforms are being made deliberately worse for customers, by their
decision-makers, until they decay completely. “Here is how platforms die: first, they are good
to their users; then they abuse their users to make things better for their business customers;
finally, they abuse those business customers to claw back all the value for themselves. Then,
they die,” wrote Doctorow in a blog post in 2023. In other words: when your experience with
a shopping app or a streaming platform grows worse, much of this enshittification can be traced
back to the dominance of just a few Big Tech players, looser antitrust enforcement by
authorities, customers’ diminished capacity to control their digital experiences, and/or the
inability of tech workers to say no to exploitative bosses, according to the author.

America’s Pentagon and Israel’s Kirya, Washington and Tel Aviv have decided to use two
separate op names for their Iran campaign – Op Epic Fury and Op Roaring Lion respectively.
Why two names? It’s all about political messaging. Having rechristened US’s department of

something that feeds into the narrative of US being No.1. Israel, meanwhile, is tapping into the

messaging is as important as cutting-edge drones. So, Op Midnight Hammer signalled a literal

new. It all started with WWI and gained prominence in WWII, when Germany under Hitler

Barbarossa – after Holy Roman Emperor Frederick I – for the German invasion of Soviet
Union.


US military began with colour-coded names such as Op Indigo – plan to prevent Nazis from
seizing Iceland – but later switched to a computerised naming system after Vietnam.
However, big ops get two-word names that are cleared by the Secretary of Defence, like Op

questions.stimulus:
LEGAL REASONING
The legal framework governing obscenity in India underwent a paradigm shift in 2014 with the
Supreme Court's judgment in Aveek Sarkar v. State of West Bengal, which discarded the
archaic Hicklin test. For over 150 years, Indian courts had relied on the English standard from
Regina v. Hicklin, which judged a work by its potential to deprave vulnerable minds based on
isolated passages. The Aveek Sarkar case arose from a published photo story featuring tennis
star Boris Becker and his fiancée, alleged to be obscene. The Supreme Court explicitly rejected
the Hicklin test as outdated and out of step with constitutional morality.


In its place, the Court adopted the "contemporary community standards" test from American
jurisprudence. The new standard reorients the inquiry: the material must be considered as a
whole to determine if it predominantly appeals to a "prurient interest"—a shameful or morbid
interest in sex. Context is king; a work cannot be condemned based on a few passages.
Furthermore, the judgment provides a safe harbour by requiring courts to consider whether the
work possesses serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value. This shift reflects a more
liberal, rational approach, recognising that not all depictions of sex are obscene.


Different media are governed by distinct frameworks. Print media operates without pre-
censorship but is subject to post-publication liability under the Indian Penal Code. In contrast,
films face a rigorous regime under the Cinematograph Act, 1952. The Act establishes the
Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC), a statutory body tasked with pre-certifying films.
Section 5B mandates that the CBFC consider a film's impact on public order, decency, and
morality. Films are certified as 'U', 'UA', or 'A'. A key principle is the "adulteration" test, where
a scene so obscene that it "adulterates" the film's theme cannot be approved, often leading to
cuts. The constitutionality of this pre-censorship was upheld in K.A. Abbas v. Union of India

 (1970), where the Supreme Court reasoned that films, due to their "mobility of image" and
 "realism," possess a greater capacity for evil impact and thus require prior restraint.

questions.stimulus:
LEGAL REASONING
The legal framework governing obscenity in India underwent a paradigm shift in 2014 with the
Supreme Court's judgment in Aveek Sarkar v. State of West Bengal, which discarded the
archaic Hicklin test. For over 150 years, Indian courts had relied on the English standard from
Regina v. Hicklin, which judged a work by its potential to deprave vulnerable minds based on
isolated passages. The Aveek Sarkar case arose from a published photo story featuring tennis
star Boris Becker and his fiancée, alleged to be obscene. The Supreme Court explicitly rejected
the Hicklin test as outdated and out of step with constitutional morality.


In its place, the Court adopted the "contemporary community standards" test from American
jurisprudence. The new standard reorients the inquiry: the material must be considered as a
whole to determine if it predominantly appeals to a "prurient interest"—a shameful or morbid
interest in sex. Context is king; a work cannot be condemned based on a few passages.
Furthermore, the judgment provides a safe harbour by requiring courts to consider whether the
work possesses serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value. This shift reflects a more
liberal, rational approach, recognising that not all depictions of sex are obscene.


Different media are governed by distinct frameworks. Print media operates without pre-
censorship but is subject to post-publication liability under the Indian Penal Code. In contrast,
films face a rigorous regime under the Cinematograph Act, 1952. The Act establishes the
Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC), a statutory body tasked with pre-certifying films.

governing the enforceability of contractual obligations. Section 9 addresses the critical aspect

presumption that a contract is capable of being specifically enforced until the contrary is
demonstrated. This provision effectively incorporates by reference the grounds enumerated in

inadequacy of pecuniary remedies for its non-transfer.

questions.stimulus:
The procedural stages that form the skeleton of a criminal trial under the Bharatiya Nagarik
Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023, apply uniformly across all trials, whether before a Sessions
Court or a Magistrate. The first critical stage is the Framing of the Charge, which serves to
inform the accused of the precise accusation. In warrant trials, this involves a formal written
document detailing the specific offense. In summons trials for lesser offenses, the court merely
states the particulars of the offense in plain language. Closely related is the Joinder of Charges,
which allows trying a person for multiple offenses in a single trial to prevent multiplicity of
proceedings, provided the offenses are committed in the same transaction or within twelve
months.


However, not all cases proceed to a full trial. Withdrawal from Prosecution allows the Public
Prosecutor, with the court's consent, to withdraw from the case for valid reasons. Additionally,
Plea Bargaining offers a pre-trial negotiation where the accused voluntarily pleads guilty in
exchange for a lesser sentence, involving a formal application and, in compoundable offenses,
a settlement with the victim.


Once a trial commences, the core proceeding is the Examination of Witnesses. This follows a
structured pattern: Examination-in-Chief by the party calling the witness, Cross-Examination
by the opposite party to test veracity, and Re-Examination by the original party to clarify
matters arising from cross-examination. The entire process is governed by rules on the
Recording of Evidence, dictating how a judge must document depositions.


After the prosecution closes its case, the court mandates the Examination of the Accused under
Section 351 of the BNSS. This compulsory stage allows the accused to explain incriminating
circumstances appearing in the evidence, though they cannot be administered an oath.
Subsequently, the accused may lead Defence Evidence, producing witnesses and documents in
their support. Following the evidence, both sides present Arguments, final oral submissions
summarizing their case. The trial culminates in the Judgment, the final decision which must be
in plain language, contain points for determination, and be pronounced in open court. In
addition to sentencing, the court may issue an Order for Compensation, directing the accused
to pay monetary relief to the victim for the loss or injury caused.

The Regulating Act of 1773 was the British Parliament's first direct intervention in the East
 India Company's Indian territories, seeking to address administrative mismanagement and
 establish central control. A cornerstone of this new structure was the reorganization of the
 Bengal government. The Act designated the Governor of Bengal as the Governor-General of
 Bengal, a position first held by Warren Hastings. To assist him and prevent absolute power,
 the Governor-General was to be aided by a council of four members, creating the Governor-
 General-in-Council. This answered the need for collective decision-making, yet the Act
 specified that all decisions were to be taken based on the majority vote of the council. This
 provision, intended as a check on the Governor-General's authority, frequently led to
 administrative deadlock.

 Madras were explicitly brought under the superintendence and control of the Governor-General
 of Bengal and his Council in matters of war and peace, a crucial step toward centralizing
 authority. In the judicial sphere, the Act provided for the establishment of a Supreme Court at
 Calcutta via charter in 1774. This court was vested with authority to try all cases, civil and
 criminal, against British subjects and their servants, creating a complex jurisdiction alongside
 existing Company courts.

 salary of the Governor-General to discourage corruption and required the Court of Directors to

questions.stimulus:
The Constituent Assembly of India, a body conceived and elected for the singular purpose of
 framing a constitution for an independent nation, represents a pivotal chapter in Indian legal
 and political history. Its origins can be traced to the intellectual and political ferment of the
 early twentieth century, with the idea first being mooted by M. N. Roy in 1934. However, the
 demand for such an assembly was formally accepted by the British government for the first
 time through the Cripps Mission of 1942, which proposed a mechanism for Indians to draft
 their own constitution. This acceptance laid the groundwork for the eventual formation of the
 Assembly under the Cabinet Mission Plan of 1946.


 The Constituent Assembly, constituted in 1946, held its inaugural session on 9 December 1946.
 It was during these early proceedings that the philosophical blueprint for the Indian Republic
 was laid down. Jawaharlal Nehru moved the historic Objectives Resolution on 13 December
 1946, a resolution that outlined the fundamental principles and the vision of the Constitution.
 This resolution, which later became the Preamble, was a momentous declaration of the
 Assembly's aims and ideals. After extensive debate and deliberation, the Objectives Resolution


CLAT 2027 Mock Test – 21                                               12 Minutes to CLAT


 was formally adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 22 January 1947, setting the moral and
 political compass for the work that lay ahead.


 The intricate task of giving legal shape to these objectives was entrusted to various committees.
 The most significant among them was the Drafting Committee, which was tasked with
 examining the vast array of materials, reports, and models to produce a coherent constitutional
 draft. This committee was composed of seven eminent jurists and scholars, whose expertise
 was instrumental in navigating the complexities of constitutional design. The committee
 worked tirelessly under the leadership of its chairman to prepare a draft that was then published,
 debated clause by clause, and subjected to intense scrutiny by the full Assembly.


 A unique aspect of the Assembly's composition was the representation of the Indian Princely
 States, which were not directly under British rule. These states were integrated into the
 constitutional framework through a process of negotiation and consultation. The
 representatives from these princely states were not elected by the public nor nominated by the
 British Crown. Instead, they were appointed by the heads or rulers of the respective princely
 states, ensuring that the diverse interests of these territories were voiced during the constitution-
 making process.

In the landmark case of State of Karnataka v. Appa Balu Ingale, the Supreme Court delivered
 a judgment that illuminated the transformative vision underlying Article 17 of the Indian
 Constitution. The case arose from incidents involving the enforcement of social disabilities
 against members of Scheduled Castes in a Karnataka village, where the accused were charged
 under the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955. Beyond determining guilt or innocence, the
 Supreme Court used this opportunity to articulate the constitutional philosophy animating the
 abolition of untouchability.


 The Court observed that Article 17 and the Protection of Civil Rights Act represent far more
 than mere penal provisions. They embody what the Court described as "a vision of social
 revolution and the foundation of a new social order." This characterization reflects the
 understanding that the Constitution sought not merely to prohibit a practice but to
 fundamentally transform the hierarchical structure of Indian society. The provision was
 intended to dismantle centuries of entrenched social discrimination and to establish human
 equality as the bedrock of the new republic.


CLAT 2027 Mock Test – 21                                              12 Minutes to CLAT


 The Supreme Court emphasized that Article 17 operates as a constitutional mandate for social
 reconstruction. It rejects the notion that untouchability is a matter of private custom or religious
 practice beyond state interference. Instead, it affirms that the Constitution possesses the
 authority to declare certain social practices illegitimate regardless of their historical antiquity
 or religious sanction. The provision represents a conscious break with the past and a
 commitment to creating a society where human dignity is not determined by birth.


 The Court further observed that the Protection of Civil Rights Act must be interpreted in light
 of this constitutional vision. It is not a penal statute to be construed strictly in favor of the
 accused, but rather a remedial measure designed to give effect to fundamental constitutional
 values. The Act translates the constitutional prohibition into enforceable legal rights, creating
 mechanisms through which victims can seek redress and perpetrators can be held accountable.


 The judgment also addressed the sociological dimensions of untouchability, recognizing that
 the practice is sustained not merely by individual acts of discrimination but by deeply
 embedded social structures. The Court acknowledged that legal prohibition alone cannot
 eradicate centuries of prejudice, but affirmed that law has a crucial role in establishing new
 norms of social conduct. By declaring untouchability unlawful, the Constitution creates the
 normative foundation upon which social reform can proceed.

questions.stimulus:
Urban parks are sometimes dismissed as luxuries — pleasant, but not essential. Yet the
 evidence tells a different story. Parks serve as natural sponges during heavy rainfall, absorbing
 water that would otherwise flood streets and homes. Trees within parks remove air pollutants
 and help cool cities by reducing the “heat island effect,” where concrete and asphalt trap
 warmth and raise temperatures. These environmental benefits directly reduce healthcare costs
 for city governments.

 Parks also shape the social fabric of a neighbourhood. Residents who live near well-maintained
 green spaces tend to interact more frequently with their neighbours, and research suggests that
 areas close to parks experience lower rates of crime. However, not every resident benefits
 equally. In many cities, wealthier, predominantly white neighbourhoods enjoy greater access
 to parks and better-quality green spaces than low-income communities and communities of
 colour. This gap matters because the health and social benefits of parks are directly linked to
 how close and accessible they are.

 Economically, parks are hardly passive assets. Businesses prefer to expand into areas with
 strong quality-of-life features, and parks are a key part of that picture. Property values in areas
 surrounding well-maintained parks rise noticeably. In one striking example from Atlanta,
 Georgia, a city plan to build an expensive underground stormwater reservoir was replaced by
 an above-ground green space with natural water features — saving the city over $16 million
 while also creating a public amenity. The lesson is clear: investing in parks is not a trade-off
 against practical urban infrastructure. It often replaces it entirely, delivering greater financial
 returns and social value to the city at a lower cost.

questions.stimulus:
Most people know that sleep is important, but many treat it as optional — something to sacrifice
 when work, study, or entertainment competes for time. This is a costly mistake. During sleep,
 the brain does not simply switch off. It actively consolidates memories, processing the
 information absorbed during the day and transferring it into long-term storage. Students who
 sleep well after studying retain more than those who stay up late reviewing the same material.

 Sleep also plays a powerful role in physical health. The body uses sleep to repair tissues,
 regulate hormones, and strengthen the immune system. During deep sleep, a specific type of
 immune cell becomes more active, which is why people who are sleep-deprived tend to fall ill
 more easily. Chronic poor sleep has been linked to a higher risk of conditions such as obesity,
 diabetes, and heart disease.

 A common objection is that some people simply function well on less sleep — that sleep needs
 are personal and vary widely. While it is true that individual needs differ slightly, researchers
 have found that most adults require seven to nine hours per night for optimal health. Those
 who believe they perform well on five or six hours are often measuring the wrong things: they
 may feel alert, but cognitive tests reveal measurable declines in their attention and decision-
 making. In short, the belief that one can train the body to need less sleep is not supported by
 the evidence.


CLAT 2027 Mock Test – 21                                             12 Minutes to CLAT


 Experts recommend consistent sleep schedules, avoiding screens in the hour before bed, and
 keeping the sleeping environment cool and dark. Screens are particularly problematic: the blue
 light they emit suppresses melatonin, the hormone that signals to the body that it is time to
 sleep. Yet even a good sleep environment cannot compensate for a cultural attitude that treats
 sleeplessness as a virtue.

 “Sleep 101”, University of Michigan School of Public Health.]
